plan.title: bug(merge): pr:wait-mergeable-and-merge --resume returns QUEUE-PENDING at once instead of waiting for the queue

narratives.Description: On a branch with a GitHub merge queue, `pr:wait-mergeable-and-merge` enqueues the PR, reads its queue state once and exits 3 while the PR is still queued; `--resume` also reads once. Workers loop the resume command or poll GitHub by hand until the queue merges or removes the PR. This story adds one opt-in `--wait` option that repeats today's queue read every 60 seconds under one deadline (`--cap-minutes`) and ends on the first non-pending result, after three failed reads in a row, or at the cap, with a stop reason in the JSON and text output. Without `--wait` nothing changes.
narratives.UserStory: As a worker agent that merges through the merge queue, I want one command that waits until the queue merges or removes my PR, so that I do not loop the resume command or poll GitHub by hand.
narratives.ImplementationPlan: One product PR (deft-story: 6423). 1. `packages/core/src/pr-wait-mergeable/constants.ts`: `MERGE_QUEUE_WAIT_POLL_SECONDS = 60` and `MERGE_QUEUE_WAIT_MAX_FAILED_READS = 3`, each with a reason comment; the operator mints the intent-constraint record for both values (see `x-directive/intentConstraint`) before the product PR. 2. `cascade.ts`: split one queue attempt out of `reportMergeQueueState` (one-read output unchanged); add the wait loop (one deadline, retry and reset rules, the latest attempt decides at the deadline) with injectable sleep and clock seams; use it from `resumeMergeQueueRead` and from the read after enqueue when `wait` is set; add `wait_stop_reason` to the queue payload of wait results only. 3. `main.ts`: parse `--wait`, pass it through, print one `wait stop:` line in text output. 4. Tests: `cascade.test.ts` for the loop criteria; `main.test.ts` for parsing, the unchanged one-read output and one JSON document; a doc contract test for `content/scm/github.md`. 5. Docs: `content/scm/github.md` Merge queue mode and the swarm `core-phase-5-6.md` cascade text; `content/docs/github-merge-queue-setup.md` Known-issues line only if #6366 has landed that file. 6. One `changelog.d/` fragment.
narratives.Overview:
1. Flag. `pr:wait-mergeable-and-merge` accepts `--wait`. It applies to the read after enqueue on the first call in merge-queue mode, and to `--resume`. Without `--wait`, behaviour, output and exit codes are unchanged. Outside merge-queue mode the flag has no effect.
2. Loop. With `--wait`, the verb makes today's queue read. When the read gives `queued` or `awaiting-admission`, the verb sleeps and reads again. The first read that gives any other result ends the wait with today's exit code and text for that result: `merged` 0 with post-merge reconciliation run once, `head-changed` 1, `removed` 1 with GitHub's reason, `inactive` 1.
3. One deadline. The deadline is the start of the wait plus `--cap-minutes` (existing flag and default). It bounds pending sleeps and failed-read retries alike. No sleep ends after the deadline, and no read starts after it.
4. Failed reads. A read that the GraphQL floor refuses, or that fails, is tried again after the interval. A read that succeeds resets the count of failed reads. Three failed reads in a row end the wait with exit 2, the read error and the resume command.
5. At the deadline the latest attempt decides. When the latest attempt was a successful read with a pending result, the verb exits 3 with today's pending result and resume command. When the latest attempt failed, the verb exits 2 with that error and the resume command. An earlier pending read is never reported as the current state.
6. Stop reason. A result produced under `--wait` carries one structured field in the `--json` output, with the values `result`, `cap` and `read-unavailable`, and one matching line in the text output. A result produced without `--wait` does not carry the field.
7. Interval. The time between reads is one named constant of 60 seconds. Each poll is today's read (one `rate_limit` probe and one GraphQL query). No new GitHub call type is added.
8. Docs. `content/scm/github.md` "Merge queue mode (#6295)" and the swarm phase text that names the resume command state the `--wait` form, the three stop reasons, and that the wait ends early when queue reads are unavailable and does not wait through a rate limit. The printed resume command stays the one-read form.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a PR in the merge queue and `--resume --wait`, when a later read gives `merged` with the expected head, then the verb exits 0 and post-merge reconciliation has run once.
- Given a PR in the merge queue and `--resume --wait`, when a later read gives `removed`, then the verb exits 1 and the output names the reason GitHub gave.
- Given `--resume --wait` and a later read with a different head, then the verb exits 1 with `head-changed` and no reconciliation runs.
- Given `--resume --wait` and a PR that stays queued, when the cap passes after a successful pending read, then the verb exits 3, prints the resume command and reports the stop reason `cap`.
- Given `--resume --wait`, a successful pending read and then a failed read as the last attempt before the cap, then the verb exits 2 with the read error and the resume command, and does not report the pending result.
- Given `--resume --wait` and three failed reads in a row before the cap, then the verb exits 2 with the stop reason `read-unavailable`.
- Given `--resume --wait`, two failed reads and then a successful pending read, then the count of failed reads starts again from zero.
- Given the first call in merge-queue mode with `--wait`, when the read after enqueue gives `queued`, then the verb waits as in the cases above.
- Given `--resume` without `--wait` and a queued PR, then the verb reads once, exits 3 and its output is the same as today, with no stop-reason field.
- Given `--wait` and `--json`, then standard output is one JSON document that carries the stop reason.
- `content/scm/github.md` states the `--wait` form, the stop reasons and the early end on unavailable reads.
narratives.Constraint:
- Waiting as the default on the first call or on `--resume` (comment 6932748336, answer 1).
- A new exit code for "cap passed" (comment 6932748336, finding 3).
- Reading the rate-limit reset time and sleeping until it (comment 6932748336, finding 2: a stronger alternative that changes the reader; not in this story).
- A REST poll of `pulls/<N>` in place of the queue read: it cannot see a removal from the queue.

## In plain English
On a branch with a GitHub merge queue, the merge command puts the PR in the queue, reads the PR once and returns. While the PR is still in the queue it returns "not merged yet" (exit 3) and prints a resume command. The resume command also reads once and returns. A queue run takes minutes, so a worker runs the resume command again and again, or polls GitHub by hand, until the PR merges. The recommended fix is one option that makes the command wait until the queue merges the PR, removes it, or a time cap passes. The open question for the critic is whether that wait is safe and complete as written below.

## Pains
- P1 — In merge-queue mode a worker has no single command that waits until the queue merges or removes the PR. `pr:wait-mergeable-and-merge` and its `--resume` form read once and exit 3 while the PR is queued, so the worker loops the resume command or polls `pulls/<N>` by hand.

## Constraints (not pains)
- The one-read form keeps its exit codes and output (issue Acceptance Criterion 3).
- A PR that the queue removes ends the wait with a non-zero exit and the reason GitHub gave (Acceptance Criterion 2).
- #6295 rule kept: never report `merged` without a head check first.

## Anchors at the dispatch SHA
- `packages/core/src/pr-wait-mergeable/main.ts` 262-268: `--resume` calls `resumeMergeQueueRead`; no wait.
- `packages/core/src/pr-wait-mergeable/cascade.ts` 168-175: `queued` and `awaiting-admission` map to `EXIT_QUEUE_PENDING`; 206-245 `reportMergeQueueState` reads once; 653 the enqueue path calls the same one read.
- `packages/core/src/pr-wait-mergeable/merge-queue.ts` 262-309: each read is one REST `rate_limit` probe plus one GraphQL query, refused under 500 GraphQL points (`rate-limited`); 334-377 `classifyQueueRead` gives one of six results.
- `packages/core/src/pr-wait-mergeable/main.ts` 250-260 and the `finally` block: the wait heartbeat refresher runs for the whole run of the verb.
- `content/scm/github.md` "Merge queue mode (#6295)": "After enqueue the verb reads the PR once" and "it repeats the read only".
- `packages/core/src/pr-wait-mergeable/main.test.ts` 353-385: the resume test asserts no monitor call.

## Recommended mechanism (the thing to critique)
- W1. One new flag, `--wait`, on `pr:wait-mergeable-and-merge`. It is valid on the first call in queue mode and with `--resume`. Without the flag nothing changes.
- W2. With `--wait`, when a read gives `queued` or `awaiting-admission`, the verb sleeps a fixed interval and reads again. It stops at the first read that gives another result, or when the cap passes. The cap is the existing `--cap-minutes` value (default 60), counted from the start of the wait.
- W3. A result other than pending keeps today's exit code and text: `merged` 0 with reconciliation run once, `head-changed` 1, `removed` 1 with GitHub's reason, `inactive` 1.
- W4. When the cap passes and the last read is still pending, the verb exits 3 with today's resume command and one added line that says the cap passed.
- W5. A read that is refused by the GraphQL floor or fails is tried again at the next interval. Three failed reads in a row end the wait with exit 2 and the resume command, as one failed read does today.
- W6. The poll interval is one named constant (60 seconds). Each poll is today's read; no new GitHub call type is added.
- W7. The printed resume command stays the one-read form. `content/scm/github.md` and the swarm phase text name `--wait` as the form a worker uses.

Questions for the critic:
1. Should the wait be the default on the first call in queue mode, with the one-read form behind a flag, or the reverse as in W1?
2. Is W5 the right rule for a failed read during a wait?
3. Is exit 3 right at the cap (W4), or does a caller need a different code to tell "cap passed" from "one read, still queued"?

## In plain English

Workers currently have to repeat the resume command while GitHub processes a queued PR. An optional blocking wait is a good, small remedy. The existing reader already checks the head before reporting a merge, distinguishes queue outcomes, and preserves a resume command.

My verdict is that the mechanism needs one correction before acceptance: it does not define what happens when the time cap expires during failed reads.

Answers to Stop 1:

1. Keep waiting opt-in. Making it the default would unexpectedly turn existing short calls into long-running processes. Default waiting would be reasonable only with an explicit compatibility change.
2. Three consecutive failed reads is a reasonable bounded retry policy, provided the deadline also bounds retries and an unavailable read never becomes a confirmed pending result. It will not reliably bridge rate-limit exhaustion.
3. Exit 3 is appropriate when the latest read successfully observed a pending PR. A separate exit code is unnecessary; a structured timeout indicator would distinguish the two forms.

### 1. blocks-the-design — Deadline expiry during read failures has no defined result

**Evidence:** At dispatch SHA `7aef28cb547ef3a4da3927f7237fccfab38cccba`, `packages/core/src/pr-wait-mergeable/cascade.ts:210–225` distinguishes unavailable reads from classified queue states and returns exit 2 for unavailable reads. `merge-queue.ts:281–308` shows both rate-limit refusal and read failure can produce that unavailable state.

**Failure mode:** A successful pending read is followed by one failed read just before the cap. W2 ends the wait at the cap, W4 only covers a pending last read, and W5 only specifies termination after three failures. Returning the older pending result hides the failed observation; waiting for three failures exceeds the cap. The same gap occurs when the first read fails and the cap is shorter than the retry interval.

**Disposition consequence:** W2/W4/W5 need a single deadline rule before binding: the deadline bounds pending sleeps and error retries; at expiry, an unavailable latest attempt returns exit 2 with the error and resume command, while a successful pending latest attempt returns exit 3. Successful reads reset the consecutive-failure count.

### 2. sharpens-framing — Three retries tolerate brief failures, not rate-limit exhaustion

**Evidence:** `packages/core/src/pr-wait-mergeable/merge-queue.ts:262–268` extracts only the remaining GraphQL points, not reset time. Lines 281–288 refuse a queue read below 500 points and explicitly recommend resuming after reset.

**Failure mode:** With the shared bucket below the floor for ten more minutes, attempts at approximately zero, one, and two minutes all refuse. A nominal 60-minute wait exits after about two minutes and still requires a worker to resume it. Concurrent workers can encounter this together.

**Disposition consequence:** W5 can remain as the thin first implementation, but its promise should explicitly include early termination when observation is unavailable. It does not guarantee waiting through rate-limit exhaustion. Reset-aware waiting is a stronger alternative, but would require extending the reader beyond W6’s unchanged-read proposal.

### 3. sharpens-framing — Timeout needs a machine-readable distinction, not another exit code

**Evidence:** `packages/core/src/pr-wait-mergeable/main.ts:299–319` has separate JSON and text output paths. `merge-queue.ts:392–409` emits queue state and the resume command but no wait-stop reason. `constants.ts:5–9` defines exit 3 as pending, which remains accurate after a successful pending observation at the cap.

**Failure mode:** W4’s “one added line” either applies only to text output, leaves JSON callers parsing prose, or risks contaminating JSON stdout if emitted independently.

**Disposition consequence:** Keep exit 3 and the existing queue outcome. For wait-mode results, add a structured timeout indicator or stop reason and render its equivalent in text. Preserve one-read output unchanged.

### 4. footnote — Verification and envelope limits

The critique used pinned `git show` reads and the supplied snapshot only; no tests, writes, installs, or posts were performed. The existing resume test at `main.test.ts:353–385` prohibits calling the monitor; its “resume must not wait” string does not independently prohibit a new queue-read loop.

The contract’s “Envelope and ceiling” section specifies the triage write-back as the single-seat round-1 ceiling, whereas this envelope names the subsequent panel deposit. I honored the explicit envelope ceiling; the additional comment contains launch metadata, not a competing critique. **Lean:** first successor lean under Stop 1 6932680717 (round 1: 1 of 1 critic posted, comment 6932748336)

## In plain English
Problem: on a branch with a merge queue, the merge command puts the PR in the queue, reads the PR once and returns "not merged yet" while the queue works. The resume command also reads once. A queue run takes minutes, so a worker runs the resume command again and again, or polls GitHub by hand, until the PR merges.

What the critic found: an opt-in wait is the right small fix, and it should stay opt-in. One gap had to be closed: the first draft did not say what the command returns when the time cap passes while GitHub reads are failing. Two points were made sharper: three retries cover a short failure but not a rate limit that lasts for minutes, and a caller that reads JSON needs a field, not a sentence, to see that the cap passed.

Solution this lean proposes: one new option, `--wait`. With it, the command reads the queue state every 60 seconds until the PR is merged, removed, changed, or no longer queued, or until the time cap passes. One deadline covers both the waiting and the retries of failed reads. At the deadline the last attempt decides: if it saw the PR still queued, the command returns "not merged yet" as today; if it could not read, the command returns the read error. It never shows an older "queued" result as the present state. Each wait result carries a stop reason as a field. Without the option the command behaves exactly as today.

What this adds: one flag, one named interval, one output field. No new gate, refusal, approval or stored state.

What it does not do:
- It does not wait through a GitHub rate limit. When three reads in a row fail, the wait ends early with the read error and the resume command, and the docs say so.
- It does not make waiting the default.
- It does not change the printed resume command, which stays the one-read form.
If confirmed, the synthesis would assert this design. There is no leftover next-build.

## Bound remedy
1. Flag. `pr:wait-mergeable-and-merge` accepts `--wait`. It applies to the read after enqueue on the first call in merge-queue mode, and to `--resume`. Without `--wait`, behaviour, output and exit codes are unchanged. Outside merge-queue mode the flag has no effect.
2. Loop. With `--wait`, the verb makes today's queue read. When the read gives `queued` or `awaiting-admission`, the verb sleeps and reads again. The first read that gives any other result ends the wait with today's exit code and text for that result: `merged` 0 with post-merge reconciliation run once, `head-changed` 1, `removed` 1 with GitHub's reason, `inactive` 1.
3. One deadline. The deadline is the start of the wait plus `--cap-minutes` (existing flag and default). It bounds pending sleeps and failed-read retries alike. No sleep ends after the deadline, and no read starts after it.
4. Failed reads. A read that the GraphQL floor refuses, or that fails, is tried again after the interval. A read that succeeds resets the count of failed reads. Three failed reads in a row end the wait with exit 2, the read error and the resume command.
5. At the deadline the latest attempt decides. When the latest attempt was a successful read with a pending result, the verb exits 3 with today's pending result and resume command. When the latest attempt failed, the verb exits 2 with that error and the resume command. An earlier pending read is never reported as the current state.
6. Stop reason. A result produced under `--wait` carries one structured field in the `--json` output, with the values `result`, `cap` and `read-unavailable`, and one matching line in the text output. A result produced without `--wait` does not carry the field.
7. Interval. The time between reads is one named constant of 60 seconds. Each poll is today's read (one `rate_limit` probe and one GraphQL query). No new GitHub call type is added.
8. Docs. `content/scm/github.md` "Merge queue mode (#6295)" and the swarm phase text that names the resume command state the `--wait` form, the three stop reasons, and that the wait ends early when queue reads are unavailable and does not wait through a rate limit. The printed resume command stays the one-read form.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Given a PR in the merge queue and `--resume --wait`, when a later read gives `merged` with the expected head, then the verb exits 0 and post-merge reconciliation has run once.
- Given a PR in the merge queue and `--resume --wait`, when a later read gives `removed`, then the verb exits 1 and the output names the reason GitHub gave.
- Given `--resume --wait` and a later read with a different head, then the verb exits 1 with `head-changed` and no reconciliation runs.
- Given `--resume --wait` and a PR that stays queued, when the cap passes after a successful pending read, then the verb exits 3, prints the resume command and reports the stop reason `cap`.
- Given `--resume --wait`, a successful pending read and then a failed read as the last attempt before the cap, then the verb exits 2 with the read error and the resume command, and does not report the pending result.
- Given `--resume --wait` and three failed reads in a row before the cap, then the verb exits 2 with the stop reason `read-unavailable`.
- Given `--resume --wait`, two failed reads and then a successful pending read, then the count of failed reads starts again from zero.
- Given the first call in merge-queue mode with `--wait`, when the read after enqueue gives `queued`, then the verb waits as in the cases above.
- Given `--resume` without `--wait` and a queued PR, then the verb reads once, exits 3 and its output is the same as today, with no stop-reason field.
- Given `--wait` and `--json`, then standard output is one JSON document that carries the stop reason.
- `content/scm/github.md` states the `--wait` form, the stop reasons and the early end on unavailable reads.

## Reject
- Waiting as the default on the first call or on `--resume` (comment 6932748336, answer 1).
- A new exit code for "cap passed" (comment 6932748336, finding 3).
- Reading the rate-limit reset time and sleeping until it (comment 6932748336, finding 2: a stronger alternative that changes the reader; not in this story).
- A REST poll of `pulls/<N>` in place of the queue read: it cannot see a removal from the queue.

| comment 6932748336 | 3. Timeout needs a machine-readable distinction, not another exit code | sharpens-framing | accept-into-contract (item 6) |

## In plain English

Problem: on a branch with a merge queue, the merge command puts the PR in the queue, reads the PR once and returns "not merged yet" while the queue works. The resume command also reads once. A queue run takes minutes, so a worker ran the resume command again and again, or polled GitHub by hand, until the PR merged.

Accepted solution: one new option, `--wait`, on the first call in merge-queue mode and on `--resume`. With it, the command reads the queue state every 60 seconds until the PR is merged, removed from the queue, changed, or no longer queued, or until the existing time cap passes. One deadline covers both the waiting and the retries of failed reads. At the deadline the last attempt decides: a successful read that still shows the PR queued returns "not merged yet" (exit 3) as today; a failed read returns the read error (exit 2). Three failed reads in a row end the wait early with the read error. Each wait result carries a stop reason as a field in the JSON output and as a line in the text output. Without the option the command behaves exactly as today.

Limits accepted: the wait does not continue through a GitHub rate limit that lasts for minutes; it ends early and prints the resume command, and the docs say so. Waiting is not the default. The design adds one flag, one named interval and one output field, and no new gate, refusal or stored state. The design was checked by reading the source at the pinned commit; no code was run. No leftover next-build.

## Problem

`pr:wait-mergeable-and-merge --resume` reads the merge-queue state once and returns. While the PR is still queued it exits 3 (QUEUE-PENDING) at once and prints the resume command again.

On origin/master (e32e58147): `packages/core/src/pr-wait-mergeable/main.ts` 262-268 calls `resumeMergeQueueRead` (`cascade.ts` 251) for `--resume`, and `cascade.ts` 171-172 maps `queued` and `awaiting-admission` to `EXIT_QUEUE_PENDING` (`constants.ts` 9). The test in `main.test.ts` 353-385 asserts that resume does not wait ("resume must not wait"). There is no flag that waits until the queue merges or ejects the PR.

So a worker calls `--resume` in a loop, or polls `repos/<owner>/<repo>/pulls/<N>` for `merged` by hand.

## Evidence

- 2026-11-16, PR #6365: QUEUE-PENDING twice, MERGED on the third resume.
- 2026-11-16, PR #6367: about 3 resumes over about 10 minutes.
- 2026-11-16, #6272 PRs #6369 and #6371: about 5 resumes each.
- 2026-11-16, #6398 completion #6403: resume returned exit 3 at once; the worker polled `merged` by hand.

Merge-queue mode came from #6295 / #6322. PR #6414 lists this as not covered by #6336.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a PR in the merge queue, when the operator runs `pr:wait-mergeable-and-merge --resume` with a wait option, then the command blocks until the PR is merged, removed from the queue, or a time cap is hit.
- Given a PR that the queue removes, when the wait ends, then the command exits non-zero and names the reason the queue gave.
- Given the existing one-read form, when it is still used, then it keeps its current exit codes.
